name: Emeka Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Walk me through a usual workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and play bass guitar in a theatre band, record short shop advert lines, and teach six adults at a community centre. I studied music at university and have handled live stages for years, though I still practise the awkward entrances before a show. The best moment is when the singer and bass land together without looking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What supports the household between shows?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a print shop, our children are grown, and we have a mortgage. Three months of bills are saved, my pay is ordinary for this work, and a few other venues hire nearby. I use AI daily to sort my own demo takes, then compare the suggested order with the music I actually played.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stage manager that a faster set list helps if every paid rehearsal and loading hour stays on it. I would still listen for the singer’s breath before coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre run, six pupils and my partner’s regular shop wages make this season workable. Three months saved covers a short break, but I keep an eye on the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the paid theatre band, six pupils and advert sessions, and ask for written rehearsal, loading and cancellation fees. In the plateau’s first year I would request an actual pension estimate and set it beside our mortgage bills before choosing any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next run because the signed work covers our bills. A set list is not a pay slip, but this one has paid hours behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask about loading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The amplifier and bass cabinet take time after the last song. I want that time on the same written fee sheet as the rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you planning to retire now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not seen a pension estimate. My partner and I would compare the actual figure with our bills before naming a date.

I would welcome **faster set lists** if rehearsals remain paid.
think: The **theatre run** and six pupils cover current bills.
Our **three-month reserve** handles a short break between shows.
do: Keep **theatre band**, six paid pupils and advert sessions this month.
Request **written rehearsal fees**, loading hours and cancellation terms.
Request an **actual pension estimate** in the plateau’s first year and compare it with mortgage bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about signed work and bills.
S0.quote: A set list is not a pay slip, but this one has paid hours behind it.
fieldNote: His **paid theatre run** and six pupils support present security with a three-month reserve.
He requests an **actual pension estimate** rather than assuming a retirement income.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre band, six pupils and advert sessions this month
Request written rehearsal/loading fees and cancellation terms
Request actual pension estimate in first plateau year; compare with mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that generated bass lines might be cheap, but the singer still needs a paid human player on stage. I would ask which advert sessions and live rehearsals are booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert lines are about a quarter of my own fees, and I expect some clients to use generated music. The theatre and pupils still pay, but I cannot treat those lost sessions as spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would get the theatre and advert dates in writing and ask for a paid engineer lesson on a new AI audio repair checker, which flags clicks and suggests repairs. In disruption’s first year I would test it only on my own nameless bass take with approved local theatre storage, compare each changed beat to the original by ear, and stop if it shifts timing or sends the file outside the theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the likely loss of advert sessions. I enjoy a new tool, but a clean bass take needs a paying order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a pupil recording to test it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Their names and playing stay in the centre folder. My own take is enough to learn whether the checker is trustworthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the engineer cannot spare a paid hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a later paid lesson and keep working from the original takes. A free trial would use time I already sell to clients.

I would say a **human bassist** still earns a live fee.
think: Generated **advert music** may remove a quarter of my own fees.
**Theatre and pupil income** would continue, but may not replace lost sessions.
do: Request **written theatre dates** and paid engineer instruction next month.
Test the **repair checker** only after paid instruction and approved local storage on my nameless take; compare beats, stop errors/leaks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely advert-fee loss.
S1.quote: I enjoy a new tool, but a clean bass take needs a paying order.
fieldNote: The **new repair checker** needs paid instruction, approved storage, his own nameless audio and ear comparison.
His **advert quarter** is at risk while live theatre and pupils still pay.

steps.text: Request written theatre/advert dates and paid engineer lesson next month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that thinking AGI in 2028 could sell an advert bass line before robot bass players arrive around 2031. I would ask the theatre for signed live calls now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the advert sessions to end in 2028. If theatre rehearsals are cut too, the centre pupils and my partner’s wages will not simply replace that music pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total paid advert invoices and get signed theatre rehearsal dates. In the first year after 2028, if advert fees end and theatre calls fall, I would apply for a posted paid community-centre bass tutor role only if the posting accepts my music degree and adult teaching record, its written net pay after travel replaces those lost fees and the last bus works; I would keep theatre and current pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected advert loss, but three months saved lets me search for a real post. I would be alarmed if most live calls disappeared too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a human tutor do when AGI can plan lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen to a beginner’s hands and stop when the bass strap hurts or a note buzzes. I already do that with adults, but the new employer still has to post a paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look in 2028 if robots come in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advert line can lose its price as soon as thinking AGI arrives. Robot players follow three years later in the card.

say: I would seek **signed live calls** before 2028.
I would separate **2028 AGI** from robot bass players around 2031.
think: I expect **advert sessions** to end in 2028, removing about a quarter of my own paid music work.
Further **theatre-call cuts** would leave a larger income gap even while the community-centre pupils continue.
do: Total **advert invoices** and secure signed theatre rehearsal dates now.
Apply for **posted bass tutor** after advert and theatre losses if degree and adult teaching qualify; require written replacement net after travel.
Keep **theatre and pupils** until signed offer and workable last bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected advert loss with time to search.
S2.quote: I would listen to a beginner’s hands and stop when the bass strap hurts or a note buzzes.
fieldNote: The **2028 advert loss** precedes capable robot bassists around 2031.
A **human tutor** corrects real playing and needs a posted paid role accepting his degree and adult teaching record.

steps.text: Total advert invoices and secure signed theatre calls this month
Apply after advert/theatre losses to posted tutor role accepting degree/teaching; written replacement net after travel
Keep paid theatre and pupils until signed offer; check last bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that five years until AGI by 2031 lets me learn live sound under a technician, with paid time. Robot bass players around 2034 are a later concern than advert fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert work could thin before 2031, and a sound job might keep me near music. A live-sound course badge is not mortgage money unless a real venue accepts it for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would enrol in a live-sound certificate only after a venue confirms a real funded place, paid training hours without losing theatre, pupil or partner wages, a last bus home and written acceptance of that certificate for its posted paid assistant job. In the first year after 2031, if advert or theatre fees fall, I would apply only if the completed certificate meets the actual posting and a written net offer after travel replaces lost fees; I would keep paid music until a signed offer and start sound checks under a technician, never running a crowded show alone before signed equipment and safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording income, but the course would be a practical next skill if somebody pays for the hours. I will not call training a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you mix a crowded show alone just after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A venue technician must supervise my first checks. I would wait for signed equipment and safety checks before handling a crowded show alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if tuition is paid but your hours are not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the theatre and pupils and ask about another intake. A free class can still cost a working day.

I would separate **2031 AGI** from robot bass players around 2034.
think: A **course badge** without a paid accepted post will not cover mortgage bills.

Apply for **posted sound assistant** after 2031 losses only if completed certificate qualifies and written replacement net after travel works.
Keep **paid music** until signed offer; begin supervised sound checks and avoid solo crowded shows before signed safety clearance.
feel: I feel **anxious** until sound training leads to paid hours.
S3.quote: A live-sound course badge is not mortgage money unless a real venue accepts it for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that ten years until AGI by 2036 gives us time to put rehearsal, loading and recording rights on paper. Robot bass players around 2039 do not settle next month’s fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer late load-outs, but I do not know what any pension would pay. The theatre and pupils pay now; advert work could be gone by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and written theatre renewal, then save one tenth of any extra paid festival fee after mortgage, food and travel toward five months of bills. In the first year after 2036 I would keep the theatre and pupils while their hours pay, and seek a posted paid arts-centre bass tutor role only if advert and theatre fees fall, its requirements accept my music degree and adult teaching, its written net pay after travel replaces the losses and the last bus fits; I would leave current paid work only with a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end of advert work while our paid theatre run holds. A long calendar is a chance to get terms in writing, not a retirement cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the extra festival fee does not arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I save nothing new from festivals that month. Five months is a goal, not the reserve we have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the pension estimate make you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare the actual amount with bills, health and the paid hours still offered. We have no retirement date set.

S4.quote: A long calendar is a chance to get terms in writing, not a retirement cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the advert bass lines could stop paying before another venue hires me. Signed theatre calls, a real tutor posting accepting my degree and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the sound checks before a new assistant handles a crowded show. A certificate should start supervised practice, not leave a new assistant alone with a crowded show.

headlineQuote: A certificate should start supervised practice, not leave a new assistant alone with a crowded show.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old bassist** with a music degree, theatre work, advert recordings and six adult pupils.
His **three-month reserve**, typical musician pay and some local venues steady the present but leave advert fees exposed.
He uses **AI daily** but learns a new repair checker only with paid instruction, approved storage and ear checks.
His **sound route** needs funded paid training, accepted certificate, supervised checks and a real replacement net offer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could erase paid advert bass lines before he finds replacement venue work.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed theatre calls**, a posted tutor vacancy accepting his degree and written net pay after travel.
